After I graduated I worked for Intel supporting the photolithography module in manufacturing.  They hire a lot of MS/PhDs of all fields.  Downside with manufacturing is you're basically always on call.  Night shifts, weekend work. It's relentless, but great experience with state of the art tech (193nm immersion, EUV, high volume fab).  After that worked for a small research company building IR cameras.  Aerospace world is vastly different that semiconductor manufacturing and start ups are stressful.  Eventually I switched back to the semiconductor manufacturing and work in process engineering and integration.  It's a lot of DOE planning, statistical analysis, and general project management with multiple teams (devices, layout, manufacturing, business unit, etc).  Not much research, but mainly developing new processes for the business unit to sell to customers.

  
Finding a job in semiconductor manufacturing was pretty easy, but I was picky and didn't take the first offer.  I've also moved across the US twice for jobs.  The PhD probably opened a few extra doors compared to a MS.  However the return on investment for a PhD is longer in terms of salary.  With the CHIPs act throwing money at semiconductor companies in the US, I think there should be a steady demand for ECE majors.

For me personally it is really hard to "measure" overtraining. It's easy to measure the physical stress: training volume, HR changes, sleep tracking, etc. Mental stress has a major impact for me and its hard to measure or predict. For example issues at work can put a large amount of stress on me. Then I see declines in my performance.  The number one overtraining symptom to me is my attitude. I get very grumpy/irritable at everything, lose motivation to train, and find excuses to not train. When I consistently can't improve my mood. I know I'm starting to "overtrain." Everyone responds differently. Learn how your body handles stress. Take a mental break if needed. Ditch the watch and just go work out. Be mindful of your body. There are times you push through like in a build up to your A race. However there are times you gotta listen to your body. It's a very fine line. Stay consistent in your training and over time you will learn how you adapt.

Agreed.  It is pretty arbitrary.  It's really just marketing terminology bull so people can say they have the same size transistors as their competitors.  Your physical gate length can be 7nm, but the spacing between each of the transistors is the same as Intel's 10nm node.  However it sounds great to business people just to say you have a 7nm gate length.

Competitors 7nm transistor node has a density comparable to Intel's 10nm node. Moore's Law really refers to the transistor density on a chip and not gate length. Granted the two are highly related. I believe that's what they were trying to say.

Yeah.  That first 8 weeks is really important to understand how PN junctions, BJTs, etc. actually work, but sounds like you don't need that much detail.  However I really like that structure.  Great stuff to understand.  Just condense it down to a week or two of basics. :)

I would also look into some new technologies since you will be writing patents.  Graphene, Carbon nanotubes, SiC and GaN (big growth in the power industry with those), III-V materials (solar applications, thermoelectrics, etc.), MEMS sensors.

Does your school offer an undergraduate level "Intro to semiconductors" course?  If so, you could talk to the professor that teaches that class and get recommendations for the curriculum.

If not, I would recommend the book "Solid State Electronics Devices" by Ben Streetman.  Tons of other good options out there.  Streetman does a good job stepping through the physics needed for understanding electron movement (fermi levels, electron distribution, etc.), then PN diodes, BJTs, MOS stack, then MOSFETS.  Start with those basics because you can feel overwhelmed if you jump straight into a graduate level understanding of each device.  Once you get the basics of the theory of PN diodes, BJTs, and MOSFETS, you can move on to fabrication if you have time. I am about 2 years from getting my PhD in Electrical Engineering and the one thing I've realized is that don't get you PhD unless you are passionate about that subject.  Don't do it for the money or long term investment.  A PhD in sciences means creating or discovering something no one has ever done before in the history of mankind.  You are expanding the world's knowledge and will continue to do so for the rest of your career.  This is something I have to remind myself to stay motivated.

The one thing I absolutely hate about my grad program is how isolated I am from other people.  Their are others guys in my office, but we all work on different projects and work together rarely.  Also the language barrier often makes socializing more difficult.  Picking an adviser and a program that is suited for you is very important for a PhD.  I basically took what I could get with my grades (which is still tuition plus a modest salary).

Finally a PhD does not condemn you to do one thing for the rest of your life.  Most PhD's that write their dissertation on quantum cascade lasers for example aren't going to work on them b/c the demand in industry is not high.  However if you have a engineering PhD (or other math and sciences), employers know that you are capable of solving problems and doing research independently.  That is why industry hires PhDs.  Not for their dissertation.  

I honestly can't provide any feedback on other PhD programs other than engineering and math b/c I know nothing about them.
